title: Neemsi: Bengaluru's Vegetarian Restaurant Sourcing Spices Straight From the Farm
excerpt: Two and a half years after opening, the pure-vegetarian restaurant runs two south Bengaluru outlets and buys whole spices directly from farmers in the regions known for them. It says the two outlets have gathered more than 20,000 Google reviews.
body:
• Neemsi buys whole spices directly from farmers in the regions known for them — cardamom from Idukki, black pepper from Wayanad and Coorg, Byadgi chillies from north Karnataka, jeera from Rajasthan and Gujarat, turmeric from Erode, and saffron from Pampore — and displays the sourcing on an in-house "Spiceology wall."
  • The pure-vegetarian restaurant opened in April 2024 with two south Bengaluru outlets — JP Nagar 6th Phase and Basavanagudi on KR Road. Its 100-plus dish menu spans North Indian, Italian, Thai, Continental and Indo-Chinese cuisines, most available Jain on request; cost for two is around ₹1,500.
  • Seasonal limited menus called "The Edit" run for a few months and are then retired; the current Festive Edit runs till 15 November 2026, timed for Navratri, Durga Puja, Dussehra and Diwali.
  • The company says its two outlets have more than 20,000 Google reviews averaging 4.8; skip.menu independently shows 4.8 across more than 8,500 reviews, and a third outlet is being planned.

A restaurant built on serving well

Neemsi is named for neem and tulsi — the tree that keeps the compound safe, and the plant offered to a guest before anything else is discussed. The pure-vegetarian restaurant, which opened in April 2024, says it runs on a single internal line: no one at a Neemsi table eats second best. Neem incense is lit at the entrance before every service at both outlets, and a house-made tulsi palate cleanser reaches the table as soon as guests sit down.

Spices from the farmer, not the wholesale market

The defining feature of the kitchen is how it buys spices. According to the restaurant, it purchases whole spices directly from farmers in the regions known for them, instead of picking up packets from a wholesale market: cardamom from Idukki in Kerala, black pepper from Wayanad and Coorg, Byadgi chillies from north Karnataka (prized for colour more than heat), jeera from Rajasthan and Gujarat, turmeric from Erode, and saffron from Pampore in Kashmir. Buying this way, the restaurant says, keeps the spice fresher with its oils intact and sends the money to the person who grew it. Inside, a "Spiceology wall" lays out the whole spices the kitchen cooks with and where each comes from. The kitchen is pure vegetarian, and most of the menu can be made Jain on request.

A menu of rebuilt classics

The regular menu runs to more than 100 dishes across North Indian, Italian, Thai, Continental and Indo-Chinese cuisines, each with what the restaurant calls a Neemsi twist. Familiar dishes are rebuilt rather than invented: Mysore Pak Cheesecake — the Mysuru sweet set into a cheesecake — is the dish regulars recommend first; dahi papdi chaat arrives with avocado; Tapri Paneer Chilli is served in a cabbage nest. The restaurant's tagline is "Veg Cuisine Redefined." Lunch service starts at noon; diners repeatedly single out the stewards in reviews, noting they will warn when a portion is big enough to share.

What diners are saying

The restaurant's biggest claim is its reviews: it says the two outlets have gathered more than 20,000 Google reviews between them, averaging 4.8. Independent listings back up the details and the appetite. TripAdvisor lists the JP Nagar address (Ground Floor, Sai Panorama, 15th Cross Road, KR Layout, Bengaluru 560078) and phone (+91 96860 60429) with a price range of ₹500 to ₹1,500. Skip.menu rates the restaurant 4.8 across more than 8,500 reviews, with the Mysore Pak Cheesecake, masala papad and veg kofta with Banarasi curry among the most-recommended dishes; diners on Wanderlog praise the food, portions and staff. The honest caveat: TripAdvisor's own aggregate is 3.7 from a handful of reviews, including one sharply negative review about service — though the brand's own numbers describe a restaurant doing something right for its core audience.

The diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the practical details matter most: a pure-vegetarian restaurant with Jain-on-request options suits mixed-diet extended families visiting Bengaluru — the restaurant itself describes Sunday tables where grandparents order Jain, grandchildren go for the Italian, and everyone shares dessert. And the Festive Edit's pitch — food for people who cannot travel home for the festivals — lands the same way for NRIs as for Bengalureans: festival food without the trip home. The Basavanagudi outlet sits at 2, Krishna Rajendra Road (Bengaluru 560004, +91 96860 60443). Both outlets serve lunch from noon to 3:30 pm and dinner from 7 to 11 pm; reservations are at neemsirestaurant.com.

What's next

A third outlet is being planned, the restaurant says. The current Festive Edit is on till 15 November 2026.

"People don't come to a restaurant only to eat. They come because it's someone's birthday, or the in-laws are visiting, or it's been a long week. Somebody has trusted us with that evening. If they leave a little happier than they came in, we've done our job. We take that responsibility very seriously."

— Founder, Neemsi
image_caption: A promotional image shows a table set with vegetarian dishes, marigold garlands and lit diyas, announcing Neemsi’s Festive Edit menu running 11 September to 15 November. The Bengaluru restaurant’s seasonal menu is timed for Navratri, Durga Puja, Dussehra and Diwali.
nri_angle: A pure-vegetarian, Jain-on-request restaurant with farm-direct sourcing gives visiting diaspora families — grandparents ordering Jain, grandchildren ordering Italian at the same table — a reliable Bengaluru option, and its Festive Edit targets people who cannot travel home for Diwali.
author: Diaspora Desk
